chapter.title: Across the pool, and staying safe

cards.body:
When you're tired in the middle of the pool, you don't have to race for the wall. You can rest on your back.

The water that holds you up in a back float isn't only near the wall. It's under you in every square metre of the pool, so **a rest is usually just one roll away**. Today you join every move into one trip across, and you learn to lie back whenever you need to.
cards.simpler: When you get tired in the middle of the pool, you don't have to hurry to the wall. You can rest on your back. The water that holds you up in a back float is not only near the wall. It is under you everywhere in the pool, so **a rest is usually just one roll away**. Today you put every move together into one trip across. You also learn to lie back whenever you need to.

cards.prompt: You're halfway across, 6 metres from both walls, with no noodle in sight. Which of these lets you rest right where you are, holding nothing?

options.text: Lie face down, hold your breath and keep still

whyNot.a: That's treading water, not resting: your arms and legs keep working the whole time.
whyNot.c: That's the front float, not a rest: it holds you up, but you can't breathe in, so it only lasts a few seconds.

cards.reteach: A rest has to let you breathe and stop working hard, both at once. On your back, your face stays out and the water does most of the holding. At most you add a gentle kick.

cards.title: Joining it up
cards.body:
Crossing the pool is four things you already know, in a row: push off and glide, start the kick, add the arms, and breathe when you need to. Slow wins. Ten calm strokes beat twenty frantic ones.

Around the middle, many beginners run short of breath before they run short of strength. So **turn onto your back**: drop one shoulder, roll, ears in the water, hips up, chest full of air. If your legs start to sink, a small, slow kick keeps them up.

Lifting your head high to gulp air doesn't work. Your head goes up like one end of a seesaw, your legs go down, and you end up half standing in the water you're trying to cross.
cards.simpler: Crossing is four things you already know: push off and glide, kick, add arms, and breathe when needed. Ten calm strokes beat twenty rushed ones. Around the middle, many beginners run short of breath before strength. So **turn onto your back**: drop a shoulder, roll, ears in, hips up, chest full of air. If your legs sink, a small, slow kick keeps them up. Don't lift your head to gulp air. Like a seesaw, head up means legs down, and you end up half standing.

cards.title: Priya's 12 metres
cards.body: Priya's pool is 12 metres wide. On her first full crossing she pushes off, glides, kicks, and at stroke 7 she runs out of breath, 6 metres from either wall. She **rolls onto her back** and stares at the ceiling: two broken lights and a faded banner for aqua aerobics. Five slow breaths later she rolls back over, finishes in 6 more strokes, and touches the far wall with breath to spare.
cards.simpler: Priya's pool is 12 metres wide. On her first full crossing she pushes off, glides, and kicks. At stroke 7 she runs out of breath, 6 metres from either wall. So she **rolls onto her back** and looks up at the ceiling: two broken lights and an old aqua aerobics banner. After five slow breaths she rolls back over. Six more strokes, and she touches the far wall with breath left over.

cards.prompt: Sam is 5 metres into an 11-metre crossing, in chest-deep water, and is suddenly short of breath. No coughing, just tired. Which move fits this chapter?

options.text: Head up, paddle hard for the nearest wall
Roll onto the back, take a few slow breaths, then carry on
Swim faster to finish before the tiredness gets worse

whyNot.a: That's the seesaw, not a rest: paddling with your head up sinks your legs and costs breath you're already short of.
whyNot.c: That's pushing through, not resting: going faster uses up breath you don't have.

cards.reteach: Short of breath means roll over. On your back your face stays out, so you can breathe slowly until you're ready to swim on.

cards.title: Your backup
cards.body:
Before she pushes off, Priya reads the marking on the pool edge: **1.2 m**, water she can stand in. A lifeguard sits in the red chair.

That's her backup, and the rule fits in one line: **tired means roll over, coughing means stand up.**
cards.simpler: Before she starts, Priya reads the sign on the pool edge: **1.2 m**. She can stand in that. A lifeguard sits in the red chair. That is her backup. The rule is short: **if you're tired, roll onto your back. If you're coughing, stand up.**

cards.body: Tom is 3 metres from the far wall and tired. He lifts his head to check how close it is, sinks a little, kicks hard, then lifts again to check. By the third look he's standing up and spluttering, 2 metres short. The sign to watch for: if you're **looking at the wall more than the pool floor**, roll over and rest first.
cards.simpler: Tom is 3 metres from the far wall and tired. He lifts his head to see how close it is, sinks a bit, kicks hard, then lifts it again to check. By the third look he is standing up and coughing, 2 metres short. Here is the warning sign: if you are **looking at the wall more than the pool floor**, roll over and rest first.

cards.prompt: A friend asks why you'd rest on your back mid-pool instead of heading for the wall. Best answer?

options.text: My back float comes with me everywhere, and resting on it lets my breathing settle
The wall is always further away than it looks, so never swim towards it
On my back I can kick harder and get there sooner

whyNot.b: That's about distance, not the reason: heading for the wall is fine, just not on your last breath.
whyNot.c: That's kicking, not resting: the point is to work as little as you can.

cards.reteach: The wall stays put. Your back float goes wherever you go, so you can get your breath back first. Then the wall is easy.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Swimming across is push, glide, kick, arms, and a breath when you need one, all done slowly. When you're tired, **roll onto your back** and let the water do most of the holding. Your backup is water you can stand in, with someone there: if you start coughing, stand up.
cards.simpler: Swimming across is push, glide, kick, arms, and a breath when you need one, all done slowly. When you get tired, **roll onto your back** and let the water do most of the holding. Your backup is water you can stand in, with someone there. If you start coughing, stand up.

cards.body:
Next time you're at the pool, in chest-deep water: swim 4 strokes, roll onto your back, float for 5 slow breaths, then tuck your knees and stand. Do it 3 times.

Next: breathing to the side, the trick that turns a width into a full 25-metre length.
cards.simpler: Next time you're at the pool, go to water that comes up to your chest. Swim 4 strokes. Then **roll onto your back** and float there for 5 slow breaths. After that, pull your knees in toward your chest and stand up. Do the whole thing 3 times. Next comes breathing to the side, the trick that turns one width into a full 25-metre length.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now swim slowly across the pool, roll onto your back to rest when tired, and stand up if you start coughing.

dubious_claims: 'a rest is always one roll away' / 'the water does the holding, anywhere in the pool': overstated. Many adult beginners, especially lean or muscular ones, find their legs sink on their back without a small flutter kick or hand movement.
'the back float works because you stop working' (exercise 3 feedback): same overstatement.
'most beginners run out of breath before they run out of strength': sounds right but has no source.
Continuity slip: card 3 says 'day-3 back float' but exercise 3 says 'the kick from chapter 5'. Days and chapters are mixed up.
Card 1 says 'The bed doesn't stop at the edges' but never explains the bed comparison in this chapter.
Exercise 3 runs to about 139 words once its feedback and reteach are counted, which breaks the 120-word card limit.
repairedFrom.why: 'Your backup' is a list of safety rules with no scene, and it adds a second idea (stand up when in trouble) that pulls the chapter away from 'roll onto your back to rest'. Exercise 2 then tests that second idea instead of the roll.
repairedFrom.fix: Turn card 6 into a two-line moment: Priya reads the '1.2 m' marking before she pushes off, and a lifeguard sits in the red chair. Put the rule in one sentence: tired means roll over, coughing means stand up. Then move the 'Next: breathing to the side' line so it comes after the try card and is the chapter's last line.
